blocks.html: Every group of people that lives together has to settle the same questions. Who keeps the peace? Who defends against attack? Who builds the roads no one family could build? Who decides a quarrel when two neighbors both say they are right? Government is the set of people and institutions with the authority to make rules for a society and to enforce them. In colonial self-government you saw Americans running their own assemblies; this course asks what all that machinery is for.

People accept rules and taxes because government can do things that are hard or impossible to do alone. It keeps order, so disputes are settled by law instead of by force. It provides security against threats from inside and outside. It supplies public goods, such as national defense, clean water systems and roads, which everyone benefits from and no one can easily be kept from using, so private sellers tend to provide too little of them. And in the American tradition it exists to protect rights. Thinkers disagree about which purpose matters most; the next topics give their arguments.

blocks.html: Once we know what government is for, the next question is who holds power. Since Aristotle, writers have sorted governments by whether one person, a few people or the many rule.

head: Who rules
Form
What it means
rows: A king or queen, usually by inheritance. An absolute monarch has unlimited power; a constitutional monarch reigns under laws made by an elected parliament.
One leader holds power by force or by setting aside the rules, with no real way for the people to remove him.
A small group, often defined by wealth, family, party or military rank, holds power.
Citizens vote on laws themselves, as in ancient Athens' assembly or a New England town meeting.
Citizens elect people to make laws for them.
Power rests with the people and is used by elected representatives; there is no hereditary monarch.

blocks.html: Two more terms describe how much a government allows. An authoritarian state concentrates power and allows no real opposition or free elections. A totalitarian state goes further: a ruling party tries to control nearly every part of public and private life, as in Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union under Stalin.

The founders feared tyranny by one ruler, and they also feared a majority that runs over everyone else. In Federalist No. 10 Madison wrote that a pure democracy, "a small number of citizens, who assemble and administer the government in person," has no cure for faction, while "A republic, by which I mean a government in which the scheme of representation takes place, opens a different prospect." So they chose representatives, elected under a written constitution that limits them.

The United States is both a representative democracy and a republic: the people rule through elected representatives, under a constitution. Direct democracy also appears inside it, in town meetings and state ballot measures.

blocks.title: Classifying a government
blocks.q: In a country, a queen inherits the throne, but an elected parliament makes the laws and chooses the prime minister. What form is it?
steps: Who makes the laws? An elected parliament, so the people rule through representatives: a representative democracy.
Is there a hereditary head of state? Yes, the queen, so it is a monarchy, but a constitutional one.
A republic has no hereditary monarch, so this is not a republic.
blocks.a: A constitutional monarchy that is also a representative democracy (not a republic).

blocks.title: Direct democracy inside a republic
blocks.q: Voters in a state approve a new law by ballot initiative. Which form of democracy is that?
steps: The voters themselves decide the law; no representative votes for them.
That is direct democracy, used here within a representative system.

blocks.html: Thinking "democracy" and "republic" are opposites. A republic is one kind of democracy: rule by the people through representatives, with no monarch. Check: ask "who makes the laws?" (the people or their representatives) and "is the head of state hereditary?" These are two separate questions.

blocks.html: Why should anyone obey a government at all? Three European writers gave answers the American founders read closely. Each starts by imagining a state of nature, life with no government, and asks what people would agree to in order to leave it. That agreement is the social contract. It builds on the forms of government you just met.

To protect natural rights: "life, liberty and estate"; it rests on consent and may be replaced if it breaks its trust
Liberty survives only when lawmaking, enforcing and judging are in separate hands

blocks.html: The thinkers start from the same picture but reach different ends. Hobbes thought the state of nature was so dangerous that people should give a sovereign nearly unlimited power. Locke thought people keep their natural rights when they form a government, so a government that violates them breaks the contract, and the people may "alter or abolish" it, as the Declaration later put it. Montesquieu supplied the design: split power so no one can abuse all of it. The American system took Locke's purpose and Montesquieu's design.

Social contract theory says legitimate government rests on the consent of the governed. Locke: government exists to protect natural rights to life, liberty and property. Montesquieu: separate the powers to protect liberty.

Jefferson's Declaration (1776) lists "Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness," changing the third item.
blocks.a: John Locke; the Declaration echoes it with "the pursuit of Happiness."

blocks.title: Tracing an idea into the Constitution

blocks.html: Saying the United States is a representative democracy leaves a question open: who really shapes the decisions? Political scientists use three models of democracy to describe it.

head: Model
Who drives decisions
Where you see it
rows: Town meetings, ballot initiatives, local school boards, petitions and protests
Many groups compete for influence, and no one group wins every time
Interest groups lobbying Congress; groups organizing on every side of an issue
A small number of wealthy, well-educated or well-connected people and groups
The Electoral College; senators chosen by state legislatures until 1913; appointed judges

blocks.html: The Constitution's authors mixed the three on purpose. They wanted the people as the source of power (the House was elected directly), but they feared hasty majorities, so they added filters such as the Senate and the Electoral College. In Federalist No. 10 Madison expected competing factions in a large republic to check one another: "Extend the sphere, and you take in a greater variety of parties and interests." That is a pluralist argument. The Anti-Federalist Brutus answered that a few representatives far from home could not know the people, a participatory worry. The debate goes on: scholars still argue over how much each model describes American politics today.

doc.title: From The Federalist No. 10
paras: Extend the sphere, and you take in a greater variety of parties and interests; you make it less probable that a majority of the whole will have a common motive to invade the rights of other citizens...

marks.text: a greater variety of parties and interests
marks.note: Many competing groups: the pluralist idea.

marks.text: less probable that a majority of the whole
marks.note: With many groups, no single faction easily dominates.

blocks.html: The models are lenses, not rival systems. Participatory: citizens take part directly. Pluralist: groups compete. Elite: a few hold outsized influence. One institution can show more than one.

blocks.title: Naming the model
blocks.q: Associations of farmers, grocery chains and shoppers each lobby Congress on a farm bill, and the final law gives each of them part of what it wanted. Which model fits?
steps: Several organized groups compete for influence.
No single group gets everything; the outcome is a bargain.
That is the pluralist model.

blocks.title: One institution, two lenses
blocks.q: Until the Seventeenth Amendment (1913), state legislatures chose U.S. senators. Which model does that reflect, and which model did the amendment move toward?
steps: Choosing senators through legislators filters the people's choice through a smaller group: the elite model.
Direct election of senators gives ordinary voters the choice: a move toward participatory democracy.
blocks.a: Elite before 1913; the amendment moved toward participatory democracy.

blocks.html: Treating the models as three governments to pick from, or as a ranking. They describe the same system from different angles, and each has defenders. Check: ask who drives the decision in that one example: many citizens, many groups, or a few people.

blocks.html: Locke argued that government exists to protect rights. Two ideas keep it to that job. Limited government: a constitution says what officials may do and what they may not. The rule of law: laws are public, apply equally to everyone, including the people who make and enforce them, and are applied through fair procedures by independent courts.

A government strong enough to protect rights is strong enough to threaten them. Madison put it this way in Federalist No. 51: "you must first enable the government to control the governed; and in the next place oblige it to control itself." Writing the rules down, making them binding on officials and letting courts enforce them is how a government is obliged to control itself.

head: Rule-of-law idea
Where it is in the Constitution
rows: No punishment for acts that were legal when done
No ex post facto laws (Article I, Sections 9 and 10)
No punishment of a person by a law instead of a trial
No bills of attainder (Article I, Sections 9 and 10)
No jailing without a reason a judge can review
The writ of habeas corpus (Article I, Section 9)
Fair procedures before the government takes life, liberty or property
Oaths to support it (Article VI); the President must "take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed" (Article II)

blocks.html: Under the rule of law, no one is above the law: the government itself is bound by it. Limited government means the constitution sets the boundaries of power.

blocks.title: Is it consistent with the rule of law?
blocks.q: A new law makes it a crime to have sold a product last year, when selling it was legal, and orders those sellers punished.
steps: The act was legal when it was done.
Punishing it afterward is an ex post facto law, which Article I forbids to Congress (Section 9) and to the states (Section 10).
blocks.a: No. It is an ex post facto law, which the Constitution forbids.

blocks.title: Officials under the law
blocks.q: In United States v. Nixon (1974) the President claimed he could keep tape recordings from a criminal trial. What did the Court decide, and why does it matter here?
steps: The Court held 8–0 that executive privilege is real but limited, and must give way to a criminal trial's specific need for evidence.
The President had to turn over the tapes, so even the highest official was bound by the law and the courts.
blocks.a: He had to turn over the tapes: the President is not above the law.

blocks.html: Thinking the rule of law means "obey whatever the government says." It means the reverse: the government must follow the law too. Check: ask whether the rule binds the officials who make and enforce it, and whether it was public before it was applied.

blocks.html: The idea that rulers are bound by law did not start in 1776. The colonists thought of themselves as English, and they claimed what they called "the rights of Englishmen," built up over five centuries. They also had more than 150 years of experience governing themselves (colonial self-government).

head: Year
Document or institution
What it contributed
rows: King John agreed that no free man would be imprisoned or harmed except by the lawful judgment of his peers or the law of the land (clause 39): the ruler is under the law
The first elected representative assembly in English America
41 male passengers agreed to "combine ourselves together into a civill Body Politick" and obey its "just and equall Laws": government by agreement
Parliament told Charles I: no taxes or forced loans without Parliament's consent, no jailing without cause shown, no quartering soldiers in homes
No taxes without Parliament; the right to petition; no standing army in peacetime without Parliament's consent; no "cruel and unusual punishments"

blocks.html: These documents shared one idea: a ruler's power has limits that ordinary people can name and hold him to, and taxes need the consent of the people's representatives. When Parliament taxed the colonies in the 1760s, colonists argued that they had no representatives there, so Parliament's taxes broke the very rights the English had won from their kings. The American protest was, in its own eyes, a defense of English liberty.

American government grew from English limits on the king (Magna Carta, the Petition of Right, the English Bill of Rights) and from colonial self-government (the House of Burgesses, the Mayflower Compact, charters and assemblies), joined by one principle: no taxation without the consent of the people's representatives.

blocks.title: Tracing a right
blocks.q: The Eighth Amendment forbids "cruel and unusual punishments." Which earlier document used the same words?
steps: Look for a document that limited the Crown's power to punish.
The English Bill of Rights (1689) declared that "excessive bail ought not to be required, nor excessive fines imposed, nor cruel and unusual punishments inflicted."
blocks.a: The English Bill of Rights of 1689.

blocks.title: Putting the roots in order
blocks.q: Order these: Mayflower Compact, Magna Carta, English Bill of Rights, House of Burgesses.
steps: Magna Carta is far older than the rest: 1215.
The House of Burgesses first met in 1619; the Mayflower Compact was signed in 1620.
The English Bill of Rights came after the Glorious Revolution, in 1689.
blocks.a: Magna Carta (1215), House of Burgesses (1619), Mayflower Compact (1620), English Bill of Rights (1689).

blocks.html: Thinking Magna Carta guaranteed rights to everyone in 1215. It protected mainly the barons and the church against King John, and it was soon annulled and reissued. Its larger meaning, that even the ruler is under the law and owes people lawful judgment, grew over centuries. Check: ask who was protected then and what it came to mean later.

blocks.html: The English idea that rulers are limited became, in 1776, an argument for leaving the empire. On July 2 the Second Continental Congress voted for independence; on July 4 it adopted the Declaration, drafted mainly by Thomas Jefferson for a Committee of Five that included John Adams and Benjamin Franklin. You met its story in U.S. History I; here we read its theory.

marks.note: Rights that cannot be given up or taken away, because they do not come from government.

blocks.html: The Declaration has four parts: an introduction ("When in the Course of human events…"); a statement of principles; a long list of grievances against "the present King of Great Britain," George III, each beginning "He has…"; and a conclusion declaring the colonies "Free and Independent States."

The grievances are the evidence for the argument. The principles say government exists to secure rights and that people may replace one that destroys them, but "not for light and transient causes." The list then tries to show "a long train of abuses": taxes "without our Consent," standing armies "without the Consent of our legislatures," trials without juries, judges "dependent on his Will alone." So the Declaration is built like a syllogism: a rule (the principles), the facts (the grievances), and a conclusion (independence).

The Declaration states that people have unalienable rights, that governments get "their just powers from the consent of the governed," and that the people may alter or abolish a government that destroys those ends. It is a statement of principles, not law that courts enforce.

blocks.title: Matching a grievance to a later protection
blocks.q: One grievance says the King deprived colonists "in many cases, of the benefits of Trial by Jury." Where did Americans later write a guarantee against that?
steps: Find the protections of jury trials in the Constitution.
Article III requires jury trials for federal crimes; the Sixth Amendment (criminal) and Seventh Amendment (civil) add more.
blocks.a: Article III and the Sixth and Seventh Amendments.

blocks.title: Principle or grievance?
blocks.q: Classify: "He has kept among us, in times of peace, Standing Armies without the Consent of our legislatures."
steps: It begins "He has," and it names a specific act of the King.
Principles are general claims about all governments; grievances are charges against this King.

blocks.html: Thinking the Declaration is law that courts enforce. Courts apply the Constitution and statutes; the Declaration is a founding statement of principles. It has been enormously influential, quoted by Lincoln at Gettysburg and by reformers ever since, but no court strikes down a law for violating it. Check: rights you can take to court are in the Constitution, mainly the Bill of Rights and later amendments.

blocks.html: Having declared that power comes from the consent of the governed, Americans had to build a government for the whole country. Their first try, the Articles of Confederation, was adopted by Congress in 1777 and in force from March 1, 1781, when Maryland ratified, until the Constitution replaced it in 1789 (its history).

Article IX (in part). The United States in Congress assembled shall never engage in a war, ... nor borrow money on the credit of the United States, nor appropriate money, ... unless nine States assent to the same...

Article XIII (in part). ... nor shall any alteration at any time hereafter be made in any of them; unless such alteration be agreed to in a Congress of the United States, and be afterwards confirmed by the legislatures of every State.

marks.note: The states, not the nation, were sovereign: a "firm league of friendship."

What it meant
rows: One house of Congress; each state one vote
Small and large states equal; no separate executive or national court system
Congress could only ask the states for money (requisitions), and they often paid little
No power to regulate trade between states

blocks.html: The design was deliberate. Americans had just fought a distant, powerful government that taxed them, so they kept power in the states. But a government that cannot tax cannot pay its soldiers or its debts, and one that cannot regulate commerce cannot settle trade wars. Hamilton called the "great and radical vice" of the Articles "the principle of LEGISLATION for STATES or GOVERNMENTS" instead of for individuals (Federalist No. 15). When Shays' Rebellion (1786–1787) broke out in Massachusetts, many leaders concluded the system needed more than repairs.

Under the Articles, Congress could make war and treaties but could not tax, not regulate interstate commerce and not enforce its laws; there was no executive and no national court system; major laws needed 9 states and amendments all 13.

blocks.title: Diagnosing a problem
blocks.q: In the 1780s Congress could not pay the interest on the war debt. Which weakness explains that?
steps: Paying debts takes money. Where did Congress's money come from?
It could only request money from the states, which often did not pay. It had no power to tax.

blocks.title: Counting votes
blocks.q: Twelve states want to amend the Articles to let Congress collect a 5 percent tax on imports; one state refuses. Does the amendment pass?
steps: Article XIII requires every state legislature to confirm an amendment.
One refusal blocks it. (Proposals like this one failed in the 1780s for that reason.)

blocks.html: Thinking the Articles created no national government. There was a Congress with real powers: it waged the war, made the Treaty of Paris (1783), and passed the Northwest Ordinance (1787). What it lacked was the power to tax, to regulate commerce and to enforce. Check: a list of the Articles' powers includes war and treaties; a list of its weaknesses starts with money.

blocks.html: The failures of the Articles brought 55 delegates from twelve states (Rhode Island stayed away) to Philadelphia from May 25 to September 17, 1787. George Washington presided; James Madison kept the fullest notes. They met to revise the Articles and instead wrote a new constitution (the story).

blocks.html: Every compromise answered a fight about power. Large states said more people deserve more votes; small states feared being swallowed. Roger Sherman and Oliver Ellsworth of Connecticut proposed giving each side one house, adopted July 16 by a single state's margin. Delegates from states with large enslaved populations wanted those people counted for seats in the House but not for taxes; Northern delegates argued the reverse. The result was a bargain that kept the Union together and wrote slavery into the Constitution without using the word. Historians still weigh what it bought and what it cost.

What it settled
Where

The President chosen by electors, neither by Congress nor directly by the people

blocks.html: The Convention's main bargains: the Great Compromise (House by population, Senate equal), the Three-Fifths Compromise, the slave trade clause (no ban before 1808) and the Electoral College. Thirty-nine delegates signed on September 17, 1787.

blocks.q: Under the original clause, a state had 400,000 free people and 100,000 enslaved people. What population counted for its House seats?
steps: Count three of every five enslaved people: 100,000 × 3/5 = 60,000.
Add the free population: 400,000 + 60,000 = 460,000.

New Jersey was small, so its plan counted states: one state, one vote. The Great Compromise used both: Virginia's rule for the House, New Jersey's for the Senate. See also Federalist No. 54, which presents the arguments over the three-fifths rule, and the ratification debate on slavery.

blocks.html: The Convention's plan went to state ratifying conventions, and a great public argument began. Its supporters called themselves Federalists; its opponents were called Anti-Federalists. Read both sides on this site: The Federalist Papers and the Anti-Federalist Papers, with the arguments set side by side in the ratification debate.

The Federalist is 85 essays signed "Publius," printed in New York newspapers from October 1787 to May 1788. Alexander Hamilton wrote about 51, James Madison about 29 and John Jay 5. The leading Anti-Federalist essays were signed Brutus, Cato, the Federal Farmer and others; George Mason and Patrick Henry argued the same side in Virginia.

doc.title: Federalist No. 10: the problem and the cure
paras: By a faction, I understand a number of citizens, whether amounting to a majority or a minority of the whole, who are united and actuated by some common impulse of passion, or of interest, adversed to the rights of other citizens, or to the permanent and aggregate interests of the community.
Liberty is to faction what air is to fire, an aliment without which it instantly expires.
The inference to which we are brought is, that the CAUSES of faction cannot be removed, and that relief is only to be sought in the means of controlling its EFFECTS.

marks.text: whether amounting to a majority or a minority
marks.note: A faction can be a majority: Madison worries about majority tyranny too.

marks.text: Liberty is to faction what air is to fire
marks.note: Removing faction would mean removing liberty: a cure worse than the disease.

marks.text: controlling its EFFECTS
marks.note: The remedy: a large republic, where many factions check each other.

blocks.cap: Read the full paper: Federalist No. 10.

blocks.html: Both sides wanted to protect liberty; they disagreed about where the danger was. Madison argued that a large republic is safer, because with "a greater variety of parties and interests" no one faction can easily become a tyrannical majority, and that within the government "Ambition must be made to counteract ambition" (Federalist No. 51). Brutus (No. I, October 18, 1787) argued the opposite: a free republic cannot work over so large and varied a country, representatives would be too few and too far from the people, and the powers to tax and to make all "necessary and proper" laws, with supreme federal courts, would leave the states nothing. Cato III made the same point about "the immense extent of territory."

Federalists: a large republic controls faction (No. 10); separated powers check each other (No. 51). Anti-Federalists: a large republic is too distant from the people, national powers would swallow the states, and a bill of rights is needed. The debate produced the Bill of Rights.

blocks.title: Who would say it?
blocks.q: "The country is too large and varied for one government to represent; the states will be consolidated into one." Federalist or Anti-Federalist?
steps: The fear of size and of "consolidation" is the Anti-Federalist case (Brutus I; the Federal Farmer called the plan a step toward "one consolidated government").

blocks.title: Reading Madison carefully
blocks.q: Does Federalist No. 10 propose to get rid of factions?
steps: Madison names two ways to remove the causes: destroy liberty, or give everyone the same opinions.
He rejects both: the first is worse than the disease, the second impossible.
So he concludes the causes "cannot be removed" and seeks to control the effects.
blocks.a: No. It aims to control their effects through a large republic.

blocks.html: Reading No. 10 as a plan to abolish factions. Madison says faction is "sown in the nature of man" and that liberty feeds it; the cure is size and representation, not suppression. Check: the key words are "controlling its EFFECTS."

blocks.cap: Ratification, 1787 to 1791.

blocks.html: The fight was close in the big states. Massachusetts, Virginia and New York ratified only after Federalists agreed that amendments would be recommended, and several conventions sent lists of them. Anti-Federalists had made the missing bill of rights their strongest point: George Mason's first objection was "There is no declaration of rights" (Objections). Hamilton answered in Federalist No. 84 that a bill of rights was unnecessary and even dangerous: "why declare that things shall not be done which there is no power to do?" Madison, once doubtful, promised amendments and in 1789 steered them through the First Congress. So the Bill of Rights was the price of ratification and a gesture of reconciliation.

Nine states made the Constitution effective (New Hampshire, June 21, 1788); the new government began in 1789; North Carolina (1789) and Rhode Island (1790) joined after. Congress proposed twelve amendments in 1789, and ten, the Bill of Rights, were ratified in 1791.

blocks.name: cv-amend
blocks.cap: The first ten amendments, 1791. One of the other two proposals of 1789, on congressional pay, was finally ratified in 1992 as the Twenty-seventh.

blocks.title: Counting to nine
blocks.q: By June 1788, eight states had ratified. Which state's vote made the Constitution effective, and why did Virginia and New York still matter?
steps: The ninth was New Hampshire, on June 21, 1788.
But Virginia and New York were large, rich and central; a union without them would hardly work. They ratified within weeks.
blocks.a: New Hampshire; Virginia and New York were too important to leave out.

blocks.title: Then three-fourths
blocks.q: In 1791 there were 14 states (Vermont joined that March). How many had to ratify the amendments under Article V?
steps: Three-fourths of 14 is 10.5.
A state cannot half-ratify, so the next whole number: 11.
Virginia was the eleventh, on December 15, 1791.

blocks.html: Thinking all thirteen states ratified at once. North Carolina rejected the Constitution in 1788 and ratified only in November 1789, after Washington was already President; Rhode Island waited until May 1790. Check the order: first Delaware, ninth New Hampshire, last Rhode Island.

blocks.html: After ratification, the Constitution became the supreme law. It opens with one sentence, the Preamble. You have already met its six goals as the purposes of government; now read it as the start of a legal document.

blocks.name: cv-doc

marks.text: We the People of the United States
marks.note: The authority comes from the people, not from the states as separate governments.

marks.text: do ordain and establish this Constitution
marks.note: The people create the government; it does not create itself.

blocks.cap: The whole Preamble.

blocks.html: Compare the Articles of Confederation, which began with the states and called the union "a firm league of friendship" among them. The Preamble, polished by Gouverneur Morris for the Committee of Style in September 1787, begins with "We the People." That choice signals popular sovereignty: the people, not the state governments, are the source of the new government's authority. Anti-Federalists noticed; Patrick Henry asked in Virginia who had authorized the delegates to say "We, the people" instead of "We, the states" (his speech of June 4, 1788).
The Preamble begins "We the People" (popular sovereignty) and lists six goals. It states purposes; it does not grant powers.

blocks.title: Is the Preamble a source of power?
blocks.q: A city argues that a rule is valid because it "promotes the general Welfare," quoting the Preamble. Does the Preamble give governments that power?
steps: The Preamble names goals; the powers of the national government are granted in the articles that follow.
In Jacobson v. Massachusetts (1905) the Court said the Preamble is not itself a source of power. (It upheld the law at issue under the state's own police power instead.)
blocks.a: No. The rule would need a power from somewhere else, such as a state's police power or a power granted in the Constitution.

blocks.title: Reading the opening words
blocks.q: What do the words "We the People" tell us about where the government's authority comes from?
steps: Who speaks in the sentence? The people.
What do they do? "ordain and establish this Constitution."
blocks.a: Authority comes from the people: popular sovereignty.

blocks.html: Thinking the Preamble grants powers, so that anything "for the general Welfare" is allowed. Courts have not treated the Preamble as a source of power. Check: when a question asks which part of the Constitution gives a power, the answer is an article and section, not the Preamble.

blocks.html: Article I comes first and is by far the longest: the framers saw the legislature as the heart of a republic. It builds on the Preamble's promise of government by the people.

head: Section
What it does
rows: All legislative powers "herein granted" go to a Congress of a Senate and a House
The House (two-year terms, by population) and the Senate (two per state, six-year terms); impeachment and impeachment trials
Elections, rules of each house, pay, and the Speech or Debate Clause
How a bill becomes law: revenue bills start in the House; the President signs or vetoes; two-thirds of each house can override

The enumerated powers: tax and spend, borrow, regulate commerce, naturalization, coin money, post offices, patents, lower courts, declare war, armies, a navy, the militia, the capital, and the Necessary and Proper Clause
Limits on Congress: no suspending habeas corpus except in rebellion or invasion, no bills of attainder or ex post facto laws, no money spent without a law, no titles of nobility
Limits on the states: no treaties, no coining money, no bills of attainder or ex post facto laws, no impairing contracts, no taxing imports

blocks.name: cv-clause
blocks.cap: Section 8 ends with Clause 18, the Necessary and Proper Clause. Tap the clauses of Section 8 to read each power.

blocks.html: Section 1 says "herein granted": Congress has only the powers the Constitution gives it, unlike a state legislature, which may pass any law its own constitution does not forbid. But no list can name every means. So Clause 18 adds the power "To make all Laws which shall be necessary and proper for carrying into Execution the foregoing Powers." A national bank, for example, is not listed, but in McCulloch v. Maryland the Court held it was a proper means of carrying out the taxing, borrowing and spending powers. Anti-Federalists feared exactly that reading (Brutus); Madison defended the clause in Federalist No. 44.

Article I creates Congress, sets the makeup of the House and Senate, lists Congress's enumerated powers in Section 8 (ending with the Necessary and Proper Clause), and limits Congress in Section 9 and the states in Section 10.

blocks.title: Find the section
blocks.q: Where in Article I is the rule that no person may be punished by an ex post facto law passed by Congress?
steps: Is it a power, or a limit? A limit.
Limits on Congress are in Section 9; limits on the states are in Section 10.
blocks.a: Article I, Section 9 (and Section 10 for the states).

blocks.title: Enumerated or implied?
blocks.q: Congress creates the Federal Reserve to manage the nation's money. Section 8 does not mention central banks. Where does the power come from?
steps: Section 8 lists coining money, regulating its value, and borrowing.
A central bank is a means of carrying out those listed powers.
Means not listed come through the Necessary and Proper Clause.
blocks.a: An implied power, through the Necessary and Proper Clause, tied to the money and borrowing powers.

blocks.html: Thinking Article I lists every single thing Congress may do. Section 8 lists the enumerated powers; the Necessary and Proper Clause adds the means to carry them out, which is why Congress can create agencies, banks and crimes that are not named. Check: an unlisted law is valid if it is a reasonable means to a listed end.

blocks.html: Article II begins: "The executive Power shall be vested in a President of the United States of America." Compare how Article I gave Congress only the powers "herein granted"; Article II uses no such words, and scholars still debate what "the executive Power" includes beyond the powers it lists.

head: Section
What it does
rows: Vests the executive power; four-year term; election by electors (the Electoral College); qualifications (natural-born citizen, 35, 14 years a resident); succession; pay; the oath

Commander in chief; written opinions from department heads; pardons for federal offenses (not impeachment); treaties with two-thirds of senators present; appointments with the Senate's advice and consent; recess appointments
State of the Union information; may convene Congress; receives ambassadors; "shall take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed"
The President, Vice President and civil officers are removed on impeachment and conviction for "Treason, Bribery, or other high Crimes and Misdemeanors"

blocks.name: cv-clause
blocks.cap: Article II, Section 2, Clause 2: treaties and appointments, both shared with the Senate.

blocks.html: The framers wanted an executive with "energy," as Hamilton put it in Federalist No. 70 ("Energy in the Executive is a leading character in the definition of good government"), but not a king. So the biggest powers are shared: the President makes treaties, but two-thirds of the senators present must agree; he nominates officers and judges, but the Senate confirms them. Hamilton spent all of Federalist No. 69 showing how the office differed from the British Crown; Anti-Federalists such as Cato IV and Patrick Henry, who said the plan "squints towards monarchy" (June 5, 1788), were not persuaded.

Article II vests "the executive Power" in a President and names powers: commander in chief, pardons, treaties (two-thirds of the Senate), appointments (Senate consent), receiving ambassadors, and the duty to "take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed."

blocks.title: Counting a treaty vote
blocks.q: All 100 senators are present for a treaty vote. What is the fewest "yes" votes that approves it?
steps: Two-thirds of the senators present: 2/3 × 100 = 66.67.
Votes come in whole numbers, so 67.

blocks.title: Alone or shared?
blocks.q: The President wants to make an ambassador of a new appointee and to grant a pardon for a federal crime. Which needs the Senate?
steps: Ambassadors are among the officers appointed "by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate."
The pardon power is the President's alone (except in cases of impeachment).
blocks.a: The ambassador needs Senate consent; the pardon does not.

blocks.html: Thinking the President can make treaties alone. A treaty needs the consent of two-thirds of the senators present. The House has no vote on treaties at all. Check: treaties and appointments are the two Article II powers with "Advice and Consent of the Senate."

blocks.html: Article III is the shortest of the three branch articles. After Article II sets up the executive, it creates the judicial branch in three sections.

head: Section
What it does
rows: "The judicial Power" goes to one supreme Court and the lower courts Congress creates; judges hold office "during good Behaviour" (in practice, for life unless impeached and removed); their pay cannot be cut

Federal courts hear cases and controversies under the Constitution, federal laws and treaties, and cases involving ambassadors, the United States, two states, or citizens of different states; the Supreme Court hears a few kinds first (original jurisdiction) and the rest on appeal; crimes are tried by jury in the state where they happened
Treason is only levying war against the United States or adhering to its enemies, giving them aid and comfort; conviction needs two witnesses to the same overt act or a confession in open court

blocks.name: cv-court
blocks.cap: The federal courts Congress has created under Article III, and a typical case's path up to the Supreme Court.

blocks.html: Why life tenure and protected pay? So judges can rule against the President, Congress or a popular majority without fearing for their jobs. Hamilton called the judiciary "the least dangerous" branch, with "neither FORCE nor WILL, but merely judgment" (Federalist No. 78). Brutus (Essays XI to XV) answered that judges no one could remove or overrule would be independent of the people and would steadily enlarge federal power. Notice what Article III leaves to Congress: how many justices, and what lower courts exist. The Judiciary Act of 1789 set six justices; the number changed several times and has been nine since 1869.

Article III creates the Supreme Court, lets Congress create lower courts, gives judges tenure "during good Behaviour" and pay that cannot be cut, defines federal jurisdiction, guarantees jury trials for crimes and defines treason narrowly.

blocks.title: Original or appellate?
blocks.q: State A sues State B over water rights in a river they share. Where does the case start?
steps: Article III gives the Supreme Court original jurisdiction where a state is a party (and in cases involving ambassadors).
So a suit between two states goes straight to the Supreme Court.
blocks.a: In the Supreme Court, under its original jurisdiction.

blocks.title: Is it treason?
blocks.q: A citizen publishes harsh criticism of a war. Under Article III, is that treason?
steps: Treason is only levying war against the United States, or adhering to its enemies and giving them aid and comfort.
Criticism is neither, and the framers wrote the definition narrowly so that treason could not be stretched to cover political opposition.

blocks.html: Thinking Article III sets the number of justices at nine. It names only "one supreme Court"; Congress sets the size by law. It was six in 1789 and has been nine since 1869. Check: if it is a number about the courts, ask whether Congress or the Constitution set it.

blocks.html: The last four articles are short, but they hold some of the Constitution's most important rules: how the states treat each other, how the Constitution changes, which law wins in a conflict, and how the whole thing took effect. They follow the three branch articles you just read, ending with Article III.

head: Article
Main rules
rows: Full faith and credit for other states' public acts, records and judgments; privileges and immunities for citizens of other states; extradition of people charged with crimes; the fugitive slave clause (made void by the Thirteenth Amendment); Congress admits new states and governs territories; a guarantee of a republican form of government
Proposed by two-thirds of both houses or by a convention called on the application of two-thirds of the states; ratified by three-fourths of the states
Confederation debts stay valid; the Supremacy Clause; officials swear to support the Constitution; "no religious Test shall ever be required" for federal office
Nine state conventions are enough to establish the Constitution among the states that ratify

marks.note: The Constitution, federal laws made under it, and treaties outrank state law.

marks.text: the Judges in every State shall be bound thereby
marks.note: State judges must apply federal law over conflicting state law.

blocks.cap: Article VI, Clause 2: the Supremacy Clause.

blocks.html: Under the Articles of Confederation, Congress could pass a rule and a state could ignore it. Article VI fixes that: valid federal law wins any conflict, and state judges are bound to say so. Note the limit in the words: federal laws "made in Pursuance" of the Constitution. A federal law that exceeds Congress's powers is not supreme. The ban on religious tests also stands out; several states then required officeholders to profess a particular faith.

Article IV: relations among the states and new states. Article V: amendments. Article VI: the Supremacy Clause, oaths, and no religious test for federal office. Article VII: ratification by nine states.

blocks.title: Which article?
blocks.q: A person charged with robbery in Ohio flees to Indiana. Which article requires Indiana to return him?
steps: Relations among the states are in Article IV.
Article IV, Section 2, the Extradition Clause: a fugitive "shall on Demand of the executive Authority of the State from which he fled, be delivered up."

blocks.title: Resolving a conflict
blocks.q: A valid federal safety law and a state law conflict. Which one controls, and which clause says so?
steps: Article VI makes the Constitution, federal laws made under it and treaties "the supreme Law of the Land."
So the valid federal law controls and the conflicting state law gives way (this is called preemption).
blocks.a: The federal law, under the Supremacy Clause of Article VI.

blocks.html: Putting the Supremacy Clause in Article I. Article I lists Congress's powers; the rule that federal law beats state law is in Article VI, Clause 2. Memory aid: Article VI comes after the amendment article (V), as if to say, "whatever the Constitution says, as amended, is supreme."

blocks.html: Having read Article I, Article II and Article III, step back and see the design: three articles, three branches, three kinds of power. This is Montesquieu's idea from the social contract thinkers, built into a structure.

blocks.name: cv-branches
blocks.cap: Three branches: Congress makes the laws, the President carries them out, the courts decide cases and what the laws mean.

blocks.html: Madison stated the fear plainly in Federalist No. 47: "The accumulation of all powers, legislative, executive, and judiciary, in the same hands, whether of one, a few, or many, and whether hereditary, self-appointed, or elective, may justly be pronounced the very definition of tyranny." Critics answered that the Constitution mixed the branches: the President vetoes laws, the Senate approves appointments. Madison replied that Montesquieu never meant the branches should have nothing to do with each other, only that no one branch should hold the whole of another's power. In Federalist No. 48 he added that written lines, "parchment barriers," are not enough: each branch needs ways to defend itself. That leads to checks and balances.

Separation of powers gives lawmaking to Congress (Article I), carrying out the laws to the President (Article II) and deciding cases to the courts (Article III), so no one branch holds all power. The branches are separate institutions that share some powers.

blocks.title: Which branch?
blocks.q: An agency of the executive branch writes detailed rules for a new law. A court later decides whether one rule goes beyond the law. Name the branch doing each job.
steps: Writing rules to carry out a statute is executing the law: the executive branch.
Deciding whether the rule fits the law is judging: the judicial branch.

blocks.title: Separate or shared?
blocks.q: Lawmaking belongs to Congress. Name one way the President takes part in it anyway.
steps: Article I, Section 7: every bill goes to the President.
The President may sign or veto it; the veto can be overridden by two-thirds of each house.
blocks.a: The veto (and signing bills); lawmaking is shared.

blocks.html: Thinking separation means the branches never share a task. They are separate institutions, with separate people (a member of Congress cannot hold another federal office at the same time), that share powers: lawmaking (the veto), appointments (Senate consent), treaties. Check: ask "who holds the office?" (always separate) and "who takes part in the decision?" (often more than one).

blocks.html: If separation of powers divides the work, checks and balances keep each branch from taking over the others. Madison's answer in Federalist No. 51 was to give each branch "the necessary constitutional means and personal motives to resist encroachments of the others."

marks.text: Ambition must be made to counteract ambition
marks.note: Each branch's officials will defend their own power, and that defense limits the others.

marks.text: If men were angels, no government would be necessary
marks.note: Government is needed because people are not angels; checks are needed because rulers are people too.

blocks.html: The design does not depend on officials being good. It assumes each branch will guard its own powers, so the ambition of one is set against the ambition of another. Every major power has a check attached: Congress makes laws, but the President can veto; Congress can override; courts can strike down unconstitutional laws; the President picks judges, but the Senate must confirm; and Congress holds the money.

blocks.html: Each branch can check the others: the veto and the override, Senate confirmation, judicial review, impeachment, Congress's control of money, and the President's power to nominate judges.

blocks.title: Actor and target
blocks.q: Congress passes a bill; the President vetoes it; both houses then pass it again by two-thirds. Name each check with its actor and target.
steps: The veto: the President (executive) checks Congress (legislative).
The override: Congress (legislative) checks the President (executive).
blocks.a: Veto: executive on legislative. Override: legislative on executive.

blocks.title: A check on the courts
blocks.q: Name two ways the other branches can check the federal courts.
steps: Appointments: the President nominates judges and the Senate confirms them.
Congress can impeach and remove judges, set up the lower courts, and propose amendments to overturn a constitutional ruling.
blocks.a: Nomination and confirmation of judges; impeachment; amendments (any two).

blocks.html: Mixing up which branch checks which. Name the check, then its actor and its target. The veto is the President checking Congress; an override is Congress checking the President; judicial review is the courts checking Congress or the President. blocks.html: Article V, summarized in the last four articles, sets out how the Constitution changes. The framers knew their work would need fixing, but they made it hard to change on a whim.

blocks.name: cv-amend
blocks.cap: Two ways to propose, two ways to ratify. Pick a route to see the votes needed.

head: Step
Way 1 (always used)
Way 2
rows: Two-thirds of both houses of Congress (290 of 435 and 67 of 100 when all members vote)
A national convention called by Congress on the application of two-thirds of the state legislatures (34 of 50); never used
Three-fourths of the state legislatures (38 of 50)
Conventions in three-fourths of the states (38 of 50); used once, for the Twenty-first Amendment (1933)

blocks.html: Why so hard? A constitution is the rule for making rules; if a bare majority could rewrite it, it would protect nothing. Requiring two supermajorities, one national and one among the states, means an amendment needs broad agreement across the country and across time. The result: more than 11,000 amendments have been introduced in Congress, Congress has sent 33 to the states, and 27 have been ratified. The Twenty-seventh, on congressional pay, was proposed in 1789 and ratified in 1992.

Amendments are proposed by two-thirds of both houses (or a convention called by two-thirds of the states, never used) and ratified by three-fourths of the states (38 of 50), by legislatures or conventions. There are 27 amendments. The President has no formal role.

blocks.title: Counting states
blocks.q: How many states must ratify an amendment today, and how many could block it?
steps: Three-fourths of 50 is 37.5; round up: 38 must ratify.
If 13 states refuse, only 37 are left: not enough. So 13 can block it.

blocks.title: Where is the President?
blocks.q: Congress passes a proposed amendment by two-thirds in both houses. Does it go to the President to sign?
steps: Article V names Congress and the states only.

In Hollingsworth v. Virginia (1798) the Supreme Court held the Eleventh Amendment validly adopted although it had never been presented to the President; Justice Chase noted that the President "has nothing to do with the proposition or adoption of amendments."
blocks.a: No. It goes straight to the states.

blocks.html: Thinking the President signs amendments or that a national vote ratifies them. The President has no formal role, and there is no national referendum: ratification is by states, through their legislatures or conventions. Check: count the steps; there are exactly two, propose and ratify, and neither belongs to the President.

blocks.html: Separation of powers splits power across the branches. Federalism splits it between levels: a national government and the states, each with its own constitution, officials and laws, both governing the same people. A unitary system (such as France or the United Kingdom) keeps sovereignty at the center; a confederation (like the Articles of Confederation) keeps it in the states; a federal system divides it.

blocks.html: The founders wanted a national government strong enough to fix the Articles' failures without swallowing the states. Madison promised in Federalist No. 45: "The powers delegated by the proposed Constitution to the federal government, are few and defined. Those which are to remain in the State governments are numerous and indefinite." In Federalist No. 39 he called the plan "neither a national nor a federal Constitution, but a composition of both." The Federal Farmer doubted it, warning that the plan aimed at "one consolidated government." Where to draw the line has been argued ever since. Scholars describe dual federalism ("layer cake": separate spheres, the main view until the 1930s) and cooperative federalism ("marble cake": the levels working together on shared programs).

Federalism divides power between levels: the nation has enumerated (and implied) powers; the Tenth Amendment reserves the rest to the states or the people; both share concurrent powers such as taxing, borrowing and making courts.

blocks.title: Classify the power
blocks.q: Issuing driver's licenses; declaring war; collecting an income tax. National, state or both?
steps: Driver's licenses are not delegated to the nation: a reserved state power.
Declaring war is enumerated in Article I, Section 8: national.
Both the nation and most states tax income: concurrent.

blocks.title: Federalism or separation of powers?
blocks.q: The Senate rejects a treaty the President signed. Is that federalism or separation of powers?
steps: Both actors are parts of the national government.
A dispute within one level, between branches, is separation of powers (here, a check).

blocks.html: Mixing up federalism with separation of powers. Federalism is vertical (nation and states); separation of powers is horizontal (Congress, President, courts at one level). Check: if a state and the nation are involved, it is federalism.

blocks.html: Two clauses tilt federalism toward the nation: the Necessary and Proper Clause (Article I, Section 8, Clause 18) and the Supremacy Clause (Article VI). Their first great test was a bank.

blocks.name: cv-case

opts.facts: Congress chartered the Second Bank of the United States in 1816. In 1818 Maryland taxed banks not chartered by the state, including the national bank's Baltimore branch. James McCulloch, the branch's cashier, refused to pay.
opts.reasoning: Chief Justice Marshall: the Constitution does not list a bank, but the power to create one is implied as a means of carrying out the powers to tax, borrow, spend and support armies. "Necessary" means useful or appropriate, not "absolutely necessary." And because "the power to tax involves the power to destroy," a state may not tax an instrument of the supreme federal government.

blocks.cap: McCulloch v. Maryland (1819). Reveal each part of the brief.

blocks.html: Article I lists powers, not every means. Marshall noticed that the Constitution uses "absolutely necessary" elsewhere (Article I, Section 10, on state inspection duties) and only "necessary" here; so "necessary" must be looser. His test: "Let the end be legitimate, let it be within the scope of the Constitution, and all means which are appropriate, which are plainly adapted to that end, which are not prohibited, but consist with the letter and spirit of the Constitution, are Constitutional." Then supremacy: if Maryland could tax the bank, it could tax it out of existence, and a state would control the nation. The ratification debate saw this coming: Brutus warned the clause would give Congress unlimited reach, and Hamilton (Federalist No. 33) and Madison (Federalist No. 44) answered that it added nothing beyond what any grant of power implies (the debate side by side).

In McCulloch v. Maryland (1819), a unanimous Court held that the Necessary and Proper Clause lets Congress choose reasonable means (a national bank) to carry out its powers, and that under the Supremacy Clause a state may not tax a federal bank.

blocks.title: Applying Marshall's test
blocks.q: Congress makes it a federal crime to rob a post office. Article I lists "post offices," not crimes. Valid?
steps: End: running post offices, an enumerated power (legitimate).
Means: protecting their property and mail with a criminal law, plainly adapted to that end and not prohibited.
So it is valid under the Necessary and Proper Clause.
blocks.a: Yes, as a necessary and proper means of carrying out the postal power.

blocks.title: Supremacy in action
blocks.q: A state passes a special tax that only federal offices in the state must pay. Under McCulloch, is it allowed?
steps: The tax targets the federal government's own operations.
"The power to tax involves the power to destroy": a state may not burden the supreme government this way.

blocks.html: Reading "necessary" as "absolutely necessary." Marshall read it as "convenient, or useful, or essential": any appropriate means plainly adapted to a legitimate end. Check: the question is never "could Congress have done without it?" but "is it a reasonable means to a listed power?" The clause still requires a listed power at the end of the chain.

blocks.cap: Broad, then narrow, then very broad, then with limits.

blocks.html: The arguments turn on one question: what counts as commerce "among the several States"? In Gibbons v. Ogden (1824) Marshall read it broadly: commerce includes navigation, so a federal coasting license beat New York's steamboat monopoly. From the 1890s to 1937 the Court drew lines (manufacturing is not commerce; local activity is for the states). Then, from 1937, it accepted regulation of any activity that, taken together, substantially affects interstate commerce: in Wickard v. Filburn (1942), wheat a farmer grew for his own animals, because millions of such farmers together affect the national market. In United States v. Lopez (1995), 5–4, the Court finally set a limit: carrying a gun near a school is not economic activity, and if it counted, Congress could regulate almost anything. Lopez named three things Congress may regulate: the channels of commerce, its instrumentalities (and people and things in it), and activities that substantially affect it.

Congress may regulate commerce "among the several States." The Court read the power broadly (Gibbons, 1824; the New Deal cases; Wickard, 1942), then set limits in United States v. Lopez (1995), which struck down a federal ban on guns near schools.

blocks.title: Applying Lopez
blocks.q: A federal law bans selling counterfeit car parts to buyers in other states. Within the commerce power?
steps: Selling goods across state lines is commerce, and the law regulates things moving in it.
That is the core of the power, not a stretch.

blocks.title: The hard case
blocks.q: A federal law makes it a crime to carry a gun within 1,000 feet of a school. What did the Court hold, and why?
steps: The government argued guns near schools hurt education and so, in the end, the economy.
The majority said that chain would let Congress regulate anything; possession of a gun near a school is not economic activity.
Four justices dissented, arguing Congress could rationally find a substantial effect on commerce.
blocks.a: Unconstitutional (Lopez, 1995, 5–4): not economic activity that substantially affects interstate commerce.

blocks.html: Thinking the Commerce Clause covers only goods crossing a state line. Since the 1940s it has covered activities that, taken together, substantially affect interstate commerce, even local ones (Wickard, Raich), with the limits Lopez and Morrison set for non-economic activity. Check: ask whether the activity is economic and whether, taken together across the country, it affects a national market.

blocks.html: Much of today's federalism runs on money. Under the commerce and taxing powers (as the last topic showed), Washington can regulate a lot directly; it shapes even more by paying states to run programs its way. This is fiscal federalism.

head: Tool
What it is
Example
rows: Money for a specific, narrow purpose, with detailed conditions ("strings")
funds to build senior centers; school lunch money
Money for a broad area, with more state discretion
Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF, 1996); community development block grants
A federal requirement states must follow
A requirement without the money to pay for it

blocks.html: Why money? The Constitution limits what Congress can order states to do (it may not "commandeer" state legislatures or officers: New York v. United States, 1992; Printz v. United States, 1997), but the Spending Clause lets it attach conditions to money states choose to take. In South Dakota v. Dole (1987) the Court, 7–2, upheld a law withholding up to 5 percent of highway funds from states with a drinking age under 21. In NFIB v. Sebelius (2012), seven justices found a limit: threatening all of a state's existing Medicaid money to force it to expand the program was coercion, not a real choice. Supporters of conditions say they let the nation pursue national goals; critics say they blur who is accountable. Both views have long histories.

Washington shapes state policy with categorical grants (narrow purposes, many strings), block grants (broad purposes, more state choice) and mandates (requirements, some unfunded). Conditions on grants are allowed if not coercive (Dole, 1987; NFIB, 2012).

blocks.title: Categorical or block?
blocks.q: A grant may be spent on "any program that helps needy families become self-supporting," as the state designs it. Which kind is it?
steps: The purpose is broad, and the state chooses the programs.
That is the mark of a block grant.

blocks.title: Is the condition valid?
blocks.q: Congress offers states a small share of new road money if they adopt a seat-belt law. A state says this is federal overreach. Under Dole, who is likely right?
steps: The condition is clear, related to the purpose (road safety) and small enough that the state has a real choice.
Dole upheld a similar condition on 5 percent of highway funds.

blocks.html: Mixing up categorical and block grants. Categorical: a narrow category, specific strings. Block: a broad block of money, wider discretion. Check: ask who decides how the money is spent in detail. If Washington does, it is categorical.

blocks.html: Federalism is not only about the nation and the states; it is also about how fifty states treat each other. Article IV (which you read earlier) sets the rules, so the states act as one country.

head: Rule
Where
What it requires
rows: Each state honors other states' public acts, records and court judgments: a court judgment won in one state can be enforced in another
A state may not discriminate against citizens of other states in fundamental matters, such as earning a living, owning property or using the courts
A person charged with a crime who flees to another state is returned on demand; since Puerto Rico v. Branstad (1987), federal courts can order a governor to comply
States may make agreements with each other, with Congress's consent, such as the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey (1921) and the Colorado River Compact (1922)

blocks.html: Without these rules, a person could escape a court judgment or a criminal charge by crossing a state line, and states could shut out each other's workers and businesses, as they had taxed each other's goods under the Articles. But the rules have limits. The Privileges and Immunities Clause protects fundamental rights. In Toomer v. Witsell (1948) the Court struck down a South Carolina license that charged nonresident shrimp boats \$2,500 and residents \$25: earning a living is fundamental. In Baldwin v. Fish and Game Commission of Montana (1978) it upheld much higher big-game hunting license fees for nonresidents: recreational hunting is not.

Article IV requires states to give full faith and credit to each other's acts and judgments, to give citizens of other states the same basic privileges and immunities, and to return people charged with crimes (extradition); states may make compacts with Congress's consent.

blocks.title: Full faith and credit
blocks.q: Pat wins a \$10,000 judgment against Lee in an Ohio court. Lee moves to Florida. Can Pat enforce it there?
steps: A court judgment is a "judicial Proceeding" under Article IV, Section 1.
Florida must give it full faith and credit; Pat registers the judgment in Florida and enforces it there.

blocks.title: Fundamental or not?
blocks.q: A state charges out-of-state residents more for a recreational fishing license. Another state bars out-of-state residents from working as electricians. Which is more likely to violate the Privileges and Immunities Clause?
steps: Recreational licenses are not fundamental (Baldwin, 1978).
Earning a living in a common trade is fundamental (Toomer, 1948).

blocks.html: Thinking a state must treat out-of-state people the same in every respect. The clause covers fundamental matters, such as earning a living; states may still charge nonresidents more for hunting licenses or public college tuition. Check: ask whether the thing denied is fundamental to the person's life and work, or a state benefit like recreation.

blocks.html: Why make them different? The House was meant to be close to the people: short terms keep members answerable at every election. The Senate was meant to be steadier: older members, longer and staggered terms, chosen at first by state legislatures, would bring "stability" and a longer view (Federalist No. 62, Federalist No. 63). Anti-Federalists answered that the House was too small to know the people and the Senate too far from them (the House and the Senate in the ratification debate). Because of the staggered terms, two-thirds of the Senate always carries over from one Congress to the next.

Senate: 30 or older (no, 28). Not eligible yet, even though her 8 years of citizenship would also fall short of 9.

9 representatives + 2 senators = 11.

blocks.html: The House is divided "according to their respective Numbers," counted in a census every ten years (Article I, Section 2). Two steps follow each census: apportionment (how many seats each state gets) and redistricting (where the lines go inside each state).

blocks.name: cv-ec
blocks.cap: Find your state. Which six states have just one seat?

blocks.html: Apportionment is arithmetic, and the House is a fixed pie. The House grew with the country until it reached 435 after the 1910 census (seated in 1913); the Reapportionment Act of 1929 fixed that number by law, and the seats are divided by a formula called the "method of equal proportions." (Alaska and Hawaii briefly raised it to 437 until the 1960 census.) So when one state grows faster than others, another state loses a seat. Redistricting is politics: state legislatures, or in some states independent commissions, draw the lines. Drawing them to help a party or group is called gerrymandering, after Massachusetts Governor Elbridge Gerry, who signed an 1812 map with a district shaped like a salamander.

head: Case
Year
Holding
rows: Courts may hear claims that legislative districts are unequal; they are not "political questions" (6–2)
Congressional districts in a state must be as nearly equal in population as practicable (6–3)
Both houses of a state legislature must have districts of equal population: "one person, one vote" (8–1)
District lines drawn mainly on the basis of race face strict scrutiny (5–4)
Claims of partisan gerrymandering are political questions that federal courts cannot decide (5–4); state courts and laws may still limit it

blocks.html: After each census the 435 seats are apportioned by population (each state gets at least one); states then draw districts, which must be nearly equal in population (Wesberry, 1964), after Baker v. Carr (1962) let courts hear such claims. Drawing lines for advantage is gerrymandering.

blocks.title: A fixed pie
blocks.q: After a census, Texas gains two seats. What happens to the size of the House?
steps: The size is fixed by law at 435.
So two seats must come from other states that grew more slowly.
blocks.a: It stays at 435; other states lose seats.

blocks.title: Two cases, two levels
blocks.q: A state's congressional districts range from 500,000 to 900,000 people. Which case is the closest precedent, and which clause did it rest on?
steps: These are districts for the U.S. House, not the state legislature.
Wesberry v. Sanders (1964) required equal congressional districts, reading Article I, Section 2 ("chosen... by the People").
Reynolds v. Sims applied the same idea to state legislatures under the Equal Protection Clause.
blocks.a: Wesberry v. Sanders, under Article I, Section 2.

blocks.html: Thinking the number of House seats grows with each census. It has been 435 since 1913 (by law since 1929), except briefly in 1959–1963. States gain or lose seats as populations shift. Check: a question that adds seats to one state must take them from another.

blocks.name: cv-branches
blocks.cap: Which branch holds this power? (Then ask: which house?)

blocks.html: Why split some powers between the houses? The framers matched each job to the body suited for it. Taxes start in the House, the chamber closest to the people, echoing "no taxation without representation." The Senate, smaller and with longer terms, was trusted with the long view: treaties, appointments and the judgment of impeachment trials, where Hamilton thought a calm, independent body was needed (Federalist No. 65). Accusing and judging were kept apart, like a grand jury and a trial court.

Congress's enumerated powers include taxing, spending, borrowing, regulating commerce, coining money, declaring war and raising armies. The House starts revenue bills and impeaches; the Senate tries impeachments, confirms appointments and approves treaties.

blocks.title: Which house?
blocks.q: The President nominates a new Secretary of State. Which house votes on the nomination, and how many votes are needed?
steps: Appointments are made "by and with the Advice and Consent of the Senate."
Confirmation needs a simple majority of senators voting.
blocks.a: The Senate, by a simple majority.

blocks.title: Accuse, then judge
blocks.q: A federal judge is accused of taking bribes. Describe the two steps to remove him.
steps: The House votes articles of impeachment, by a simple majority.
The Senate holds a trial; conviction and removal need two-thirds of senators present.

blocks.html: Mixing up the houses' special powers. The House impeaches (accuses); the Senate tries. The Senate, not the House, confirms appointments and approves treaties; the House, not the Senate, starts revenue bills. Check: "money starts in the House; people and treaties go to the Senate."

blocks.html: A chamber of 435, or of 100, cannot run itself. The Constitution names only a few officers; the political parties built the rest. Each leader uses the powers of Congress through the chamber's rules.

Chosen by

blocks.html: The Constitution says only that the House "shall chuse their Speaker and other Officers," that the Vice President is President of the Senate with a vote only when the senators "be equally divided," and that the Senate chooses a President pro tempore (Article I, Sections 2 and 3). Everything else, majority leaders, whips, the party conferences, grew out of the party system in the 1800s and 1900s. That is why the House's Speaker is so strong (the House runs on majority rule) while the Senate's leader works mainly by scheduling and by the custom of being recognized first: in the Senate, any member can slow things down.

The Speaker, chosen by the House, leads it; majority and minority leaders and whips organize each party; the Vice President presides over the Senate and votes only to break ties; the President pro tempore presides in the VP's absence; the Senate majority leader sets the agenda.

blocks.title: A tie in the Senate
blocks.q: The Senate splits 50–50 on a bill. What happens?
steps: Article I, Section 3: the Vice President votes when the Senate is "equally divided."
If the Vice President votes yes, it passes 51–50; if no, it fails.
blocks.a: The Vice President may cast the tie-breaking vote.

blocks.title: Who does what?
blocks.q: A member is told by a party leader that the vote on Thursday will be close and that the party needs her. Who is likely calling?
steps: Counting votes and rounding up members is the whip's job.

blocks.html: Committees do the detailed work: they hold hearings (witnesses, experts, agency officials), then mark up the bill (rewrite it line by line) and vote whether to report it to the full chamber. They also gatekeep. A chair who does not schedule a bill can let it die quietly, and roughly nine of every ten bills introduced never get past committee. The House has an escape hatch: a discharge petition signed by 218 members (a majority) can force a bill to the floor, though few succeed. Members seek seats on committees that matter to their districts, and the majority party holds most seats and every chair.

Most work happens in committees: standing (permanent, by subject), select or special (temporary), joint (both houses) and conference (to settle House–Senate differences). Committees hold hearings and mark up bills; most bills die there.

blocks.title: Which kind?
blocks.q: The House passed a highway bill; the Senate passed a different version. A group from both chambers meets to write one text. What kind of committee is that?
steps: Temporary, both houses, one bill, settling differences: a conference committee.

blocks.title: Forcing a vote
blocks.q: A bill has 230 cosponsors in the House, but the committee chair refuses to act. What can its supporters do?
steps: They can file a discharge petition.
If 218 members sign it, the bill can be brought to the floor without the committee.

blocks.html: Thinking every bill gets a vote on the floor. Most bills die in committee without a vote. Check: a bill's path has a gate at the committee step; only bills a committee reports (or that are discharged) reach the floor.

blocks.html: Put committees, the floor and the President together and you have the path of a bill. Article I, Section 7 sets the rules for the end of the path; the chambers' rules set the rest.

items: Introduced by a member (revenue bills must start in the House).
Committee: hearings, markup, a vote to report it.
Floor: debate and a vote; a simple majority passes it (in the Senate, ending debate usually takes 60 votes).
The other chamber does the same.
One text: differences are settled by a conference committee or by amendments passed back and forth.
The President has ten days (Sundays excepted) to sign it, veto it, or do nothing.

blocks.html: The ending depends on what the President does, and on whether Congress is still in session. Sign: it is law. Veto: it goes back with objections, and two-thirds of each house can override. Do nothing for ten days (Sundays excepted) while Congress is in session: it becomes law without a signature. But if Congress has adjourned during those ten days, the President cannot return it, so it dies: a pocket veto, which Congress cannot override. The framers wanted the President to have a real but limited say: Hamilton defended the "qualified negative" in Federalist No. 73.

A bill must pass both houses in the same words, then the President signs it, vetoes it (Congress may override by two-thirds of each house) or lets it become law without a signature after ten days (Sundays excepted) while Congress is in session. If Congress adjourns first, the unsigned bill dies: a pocket veto.

blocks.title: Count the days
blocks.q: A bill reaches the President on a Monday, and Congress stays in session. The President does nothing. When does it become law?
steps: Count ten days, skipping Sundays: Tue 1, Wed 2, Thu 3, Fri 4, Sat 5, (Sun skipped), Mon 6, Tue 7, Wed 8, Thu 9, Fri 10.
After the tenth day it becomes law without a signature.
blocks.a: After the second Friday, without the President's signature.

blocks.title: Override math
blocks.q: The President vetoes a bill. The House votes 300–135 to override and the Senate 64–36. Does the bill become law?
steps: Each house needs two-thirds of those voting.
House: 300 of 435 is above 290, two-thirds. Senate: 64 of 100 is below 67.
The Senate falls short, so the veto stands.
blocks.a: No. The veto is sustained in the Senate.

blocks.html: Thinking an unsigned bill always becomes law after ten days. That is true only while Congress is in session. If Congress adjourns during the ten days, the bill dies: a pocket veto. Check: ask two questions: did the President sign or veto? If neither, was Congress still in session at the end of the ten days?

blocks.html: The filibuster is a product of rules, not of the Constitution. The Senate adopted cloture (Rule XXII) in 1917, requiring two-thirds; in 1975 it lowered the bar to three-fifths of senators. Today a senator rarely needs to talk for hours; the threat of a filibuster is enough, so most major bills need 60 votes. There are exceptions written into law or rules: budget reconciliation bills (under the Congressional Budget Act of 1974) have debate capped at 20 hours and pass by majority, and since 2013 (executive and lower-court nominations) and 2017 (Supreme Court) nominations have needed only a majority to end debate. The debate over the filibuster itself is old. Supporters say it protects the minority, forces compromise and keeps the Senate deliberate; critics say it lets a minority block what a majority wants and makes the Senate less accountable.

The House Rules Committee sets limits on debate and amendments; in the Senate, debate is unlimited unless 60 senators vote for cloture, so a minority can block many bills by filibuster. Reconciliation and nominations have special majority rules.

blocks.q: A bill has 57 supporters and 43 opponents in the Senate. Opponents filibuster. Can the bill pass?
steps: Cloture needs 60.
57 is three short, so debate cannot be ended and the bill stalls, unless it qualifies for reconciliation or supporters change the rules.

blocks.title: Which rule applies?
blocks.q: The Senate is voting on a nominee for a federal appeals court. How many votes are needed to end debate?
steps: Since 2013, cloture on executive and lower-court nominations takes a simple majority.

blocks.html: The yearly process runs on a calendar. The President proposes a budget early in the year; the Budget Committees write a budget resolution (under the Congressional Budget Act of 1974, which also created the Congressional Budget Office); the Appropriations Committees' 12 subcommittees write the spending bills, due before the fiscal year starts on October 1. When they are late, Congress passes a continuing resolution to keep money flowing; if neither passes, unfunded agencies shut down. Notice what the yearly fight is about: only the discretionary part. Mandatory spending and interest run on automatically. Congress also watches how money is spent: that is oversight, through hearings, investigations, subpoenas, audits and the threat of cutting funds. Pork barrel spending (projects aimed at one district, called earmarks) and logrolling ("vote for my project and I'll vote for yours") describe the trading that helps bills pass; defenders call it representing constituents, critics call it waste.

Congress controls spending: discretionary spending is set each year by appropriations; mandatory spending (Social Security, Medicare, interest) runs under existing laws. Congress oversees agencies through hearings, investigations and funding.

blocks.title: Mandatory or discretionary?
blocks.q: Next year more people turn 65 and claim Social Security. Does Congress have to pass a new law for them to be paid?
steps: Social Security benefits are set by existing law for everyone who qualifies.
