blocks.q: How many state legislatures have only one house?
steps: 49 states have two houses.

What it does

blocks.html: Where do local governments get their power? From their state. Unlike states, which hold powers of their own under the Constitution, cities and counties are created by state law. Under Dillon's Rule, named for an Iowa judge who wrote in 1868, a local government has only the powers the state gives it, plainly or by clear implication. Many states also grant home rule, letting cities write their own charters and act on local matters unless state law says otherwise. Cities organize their governments in two main ways:

head: Form
Who runs the city day to day
rows: an elected mayor heads the executive branch (a "strong mayor" hires and fires department heads and can veto); an elected council makes the laws
an elected council makes policy and hires a professional city manager to run the city; the mayor, if any, leads the council

blocks.html: Counties, cities and towns, school districts and special districts provide many services. Cities use a mayor-council or a council-manager form. Local governments get their powers from the state (Dillon's Rule; home rule where granted).

blocks.title: Which form?
blocks.q: A city council hires a trained administrator to manage departments and prepare the budget. Which form is this?
steps: A council hiring a professional manager is the council-manager form.

blocks.title: Who wins?
blocks.q: A city passes a rule that conflicts with a state law on the same subject. Which prevails, in general?
steps: Cities are created by the state and act under its authority.
Where state law covers the matter, it generally controls.

blocks.html: Thinking cities are independent like states. A state is a sovereign member of the Union; a city is created by its state and has only the powers the state grants. Check: could the state legislature change the city's powers? Yes; that shows where the power comes from.

blocks.html: The national government is a representative democracy: voters choose officials, and the officials make the laws. Many states add tools of direct democracy, adopted mostly during the Progressive Era (South Dakota was first, in 1898).

head: Tool
Who starts it
What happens
rows: voters, by petition (gathering a set number of signatures)
a proposed law or state constitutional amendment goes on the ballot, and voters decide; about half the states allow some form
usually the legislature (or, in a "popular referendum," voters petitioning against a new law)
voters approve or reject a measure the legislature passed or referred; many state constitutions require a referendum for amendments or bonds
a special election may remove an official before the term ends; 19 states allow recall of state officials

blocks.html: Supporters say these tools let citizens act when legislatures will not, check special interests and keep officials answerable. Critics say ballot measures can be confusing, are shaped by whoever pays for signature drives and ads, and skip the committee work and compromise of a legislature. Recalls are rare but sometimes succeed: California voters recalled Governor Gray Davis in 2003, while a recall attempt against Governor Scott Walker of Wisconsin (2012) failed. There is no national initiative or referendum: federal laws are made only by Congress and the President, and amendments only by Article V.

blocks.html: The Constitution names three kinds of governments in one clause: Congress may regulate commerce "with foreign Nations, and among the several States, and with the Indian Tribes" (Article I, Section 8). Tribal nations are neither foreign countries nor parts of states. They are sovereign governments that existed before the United States.

head: Tribal nations today
rows: 575 federally recognized tribes (as of 2026), plus others recognized only by states
their own constitutions, councils, chairs or chiefs, police and courts

blocks.html: Chief Justice John Marshall described tribes in 1831 as "domestic dependent nations." In Worcester v. Georgia (1832), the Court held that Georgia's laws had no force within Cherokee lands, which were governed by treaty and federal law; Georgia did not comply, and the Cherokee were later forced west on the Trail of Tears. Federal policy swung for a century and a half: removal, allotment of tribal lands, boarding schools meant to erase Native cultures, the Indian Reorganization Act (1934), attempts to "terminate" tribes in the 1950s, and since the 1970s a policy of self-determination, with tribes running their own programs. Today tribes govern their members and lands, and state law generally has limited reach on reservations, but Congress holds broad power over Indian affairs. In McGirt v. Oklahoma (2020) the Court held 5 to 4 that the Muscogee (Creek) reservation was never ended by Congress, so the state could not prosecute certain crimes there.

blocks.html: Why a time line? The most common slip is mixing up dates and documents: 1776 (the Declaration, which said the colonies were free) and 1787 (the Constitution, which set up the government). Put each answer on the line and it becomes a story with causes: the taxes and the Declaration, the weak Articles and the Constitution, slavery and the Civil War, the Depression and the New Deal, Pearl Harbor and World War II. Remember the symbols by their meaning: the stripes count the first 13 colonies and stay at 13; the stars count the states and grew to 50 when Hawaii joined in 1959; Memorial Day honors soldiers who died in military service, and Veterans Day honors everyone who has served.

Anchor each history answer on a time line: 1776 Declaration, 1787 Constitution, 1803 Louisiana Purchase, 1861 to 1865 Civil War, 1920 women's vote, 1941 Pearl Harbor, 2001 September 11. Learn symbols and holidays by what they mean.

blocks.title: Which document?
blocks.q: Which document said the colonies were free from Britain, and when was it adopted?
steps: The Declaration of Independence announced independence.
It was adopted on July 4, 1776. (The Constitution came in 1787.)

blocks.title: Why 13?
blocks.q: Why does the flag have 13 stripes?
steps: The stripes stand for the 13 original colonies.
Stars, not stripes, were added for new states.

blocks.html: Mixing up dates and documents, such as 1776 and 1787 or the Declaration and the Constitution. Anchor each answer on a time line: the Declaration (1776) came first and said why the colonies broke away; the Constitution (1787) came eleven years later and set up the government.
